To enhance the performance of optimization heuristics, greater attention is being devoted to hyperparameter optimization, a need driven by the increasing number of parameters present in modern deep neural networks. Although global sensitivity analysis (GSA) has long been utilized for global variable interdependency assessment in machine learning variables, its application for evaluating hyperparameter influence within specific algorithms remains largely unexplored, with only one prior study addressing this niche. This research investigates how effectively GSA methods can evaluate hyperparameter influence and interact while also aiding in their optimization. Specifically, we applied the Fourier Amplitude Sensitivity Estimation (FAST) method to analyze the influence and interplay of hyperparameters in the well-established UCKP benchmarking instance of the discrete optimization tool known as the genetic algorithm. Our findings reveal two key aspects: (1) there is a lack of consensus on defining discrete hyperparameters within sensitivity analysis, and (2) fast fails to capture second-order correlations among these parameters effectively. Our results highlight specific hyperparameters that have a major impact on solution quality, allowing us to reduce their total from ten to just three without compromising the solution's quality.

This paper explores several proof strategies for the equivalence of two quantum mechanical frameworks based on the second-order wave equation: Schrödinger quantum mechanics (SM) utilizing wavefunctions, and wave quantum mechanics (WM) based on wave-intensity waves. We establish that these two systems are mathematically equivalent under the conditions that their initial value problems satisfy specific relationships. Additionally, these equivalences hold when transformations are established through the known relations of their respective initial conditions. Some assertions represent original contributions to the field, while others derive from current equivalent theories or result from the identified mathematical connections. Some assertions highlight features of WM not previously emphasized in SM literature, even though their connection to SM theory is rigorous. The relationships governing the equivalences of initial conditions facilitate interpretations that link WM concepts directly to standard SM interpretations. Finally, these mathematical assertions have broad applications across various quantum theoretical models.

Current reinforcement learning (RL) agents often struggle with poor sample efficiency and generalizability, limiting their practical application. To bridge this divide, we introduce L2Explorer, a unified platform engineered to facilitate experiment guidance, data sharing, and cross-lab research collaboration. This framework features an extensive catalog of domains, environments, and real-world RL benchmarks. It also provides robust support for experiments throughout their lifecycle, including pre-configured RL agents pre-trained with industry data, customizable search engines, configurable hyperparameters, agent documentation, and result visualization. Furthermore, the L22Explorer enables researchers to benchmark their methodologies against each other by providing direct access to existing data and implemented RL policies. Our ecosystem encompasses environments from RC2, River, MuJoCo, PyBullet, and real-world applications from Uber, LinkedIn, and Leasing.com, in addition to over 20 pre-implemented industry-inspired agents.

We introduce a configuration-aware safe control architecture ensuring that safe operation is maintained despite disturbances and uncertainty by ensuring forward invariance of the safe set. We develop a model for the robotic limb and define its safe operational region using Control Barrier Functions (CBFs). To adaptively handle both uncertain dynamics and external forces, we incorporate an adaptive disturbance observer. Furthermore, we formulate a terminal-constrained optimal problem to guide the safe trajectory of the limb. By integrating these elements, we transform ensuring safety into a linearly constrained LQR problem solvable in real-time. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed scheme successfully ensures safe operation for the robotic limb under uncertain conditions regarding dynamics, geometry, and environmental interactions.

Natural language processing is a critical area of computer science research. As the volume of data continues to rise, automated text analysis tools have become increasingly indispensable for interpreting natural language. This paper presents an extractive approach to text summarization, which operates by converting text articles into directed graphs, analyzing their structural properties, and selecting sentences based on specific metrics. We evaluate the system using various extractive algorithms, each relying on different sentence selection criteria, and compare the results against human-generated summaries. Additionally, we discuss potential applications of this system in news aggregation.

In the study of Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs), operators with modified commutation relations have been instrumental in revealing fundamental properties of the system. This research introduces a set of nonlinear creation and annihilation operators, whose communication relations are determined by a parameter $\lambda$. As this $\lambda$ approaches zero, standard quantum mechanics is recovered. When applied with $\lambda = -1$, these operators align with the framework of single-particle su(1,1) quantum mechanics, whereas values of $\lambda > 0$ facilitate an $s$-boson description of a BEC subject to nonlinear interactions. For coherent states constructed using these nonlinear operators, we derive their time-dependent expectation values. The resulting expressions for the average number of quanta and number operator variance confirm that this nonlinear $s$-boson model generates an effective nonlinearity capable of accounting for mean-field behavior in the macroscopic wave function of a nonlinear BEC.

Identifying the nondegenerate region of a polynomial system is fundamental to numerous algorithmic approaches, including Monte Carlo sampling, Groebner basis computation, and global optimization. This study introduces an efficient technique to determine such regions based on polynomial signatory vectors. The core concept involves transforming the original polynomial system into a corresponding system of transformed polynomials with nondegenerate coefficients. By estimating the magnitude of these transformed parameters, we derive bounds for key geometric attributes of the resulting algebraical variety, specifically hyper-rectangular spans and their associated isolation boxes around isolated roots. We further develop global optimization algorithms to compute tight bounds given any initial feasible estimate of the polynomial. The proposed framework was evaluated for robustness and speed, demonstrating its effectiveness.

At the RHIC facility, interactions occurring among various nuclear systems were recorded during experiments conducted under $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV conditions, specifically including copper+copper collisions. Research into immediate photons emitted from these events provides a means to investigate the equation of state for quark-gluon plasma and to detect the quark-gluon transition zone via thermodynamics. Because no clear qualitative differences in photon yields were observed between various collision centralities, a new methodology termed Low-Momentum Immediate Photon (LMIP) analysis has been developed to differentiate between them. This strategy focuses on isolating specific regions in transverse momentum where LM or non-charge exchange processes are more prominent, thereby enabling a refined analysis of the collision dynamics. Experimental results indicate a higher proportion of LM or non-charge exchange processes in more central collisions, a finding that aligns well with theoretical predictions regarding hard processes as presented in our research. This study reports experimental data concerning this analysis.

This paper fully resolves the $\ell_2$-metric Tur\'an number for the tetrahedron, marking the first complete solution in unit-norm dimensions. We establish that the extremal configurations consist of two unit-norm vectors spanning a subspace, with all other positions filled by linear combinations of these basis vectors also constrained to have unit norm. While the original $\ell_1$ solution involved a triangle of unit vectors with all other points as their midpoints, we demonstrate its non-extremality in the $\ell_2$-setting unless such midpoints are replaced by unit-unit vectors. Several properties of the resulting structure are analyzed, with specific focus on the case where the unit norm dimensions reduce to those of two.

When rendering thin vector lines at lower resolutions by connecting map points across effective anti-aliasing space, we can ensure a smoother visual experience without over-computation. To achieve this balance between rendering quality and performance, particularly when lines are minimal in width relative to the screen, we employ a technique that offers both quantitative and qualitative anti-aliasing solutions. Our approach involves a two-stage process: initially, we construct an Anti-Aliasing Line Connection Table (AALC) featuring pre-calculated anti-aliased segments for every pair of map points; subsequently, we utilize simple table look-up operations to establish actual lines by simply selecting the entry corresponding to each connected pair. This method eliminates the need for complex algorithmic computations during the final rendering stage while simultaneously generating high-quality anti-aliased lines. To further enhance visual fidelity, each pre-calused line is rendered using the specific screen depth at which it was originally generated, with the input map points rendered at full screen resolution to complete the visualization.

This paper introduces a new quasi-interpolation scheme derived from forms conserving theory, utilizing a novel transcendental radial basis function (RBF). This study presents a catalog containing 110 gamma-ray shells attributed to expanding pulsar wind. Located within our Galaxy, this collection was assembled by analyzing data from multiple missions, including Fermi-LAT, AGILE, HESS, MAGIC, CTAEROS, and BATSE. The resulting catalog exhibits greater size and an improved refinement of object parameters—specifically coordinates, longitudes of magnetic fields, and expansion velocities—when compared to the most recent catalog compiled by Mitton et al. (2013). Spatial analysis indicates a non-uniform distribution of these shells relative to the Galaxy's plane; rather than following the classic "disk-sphere" model, shells associated with younger pulsars appear more prevalent at higher galactic latitudes. Although the total count has increased, this new catalog still likely misses many shells because current instruments cannot detect the fainter emission from expanding shells in the MeV range.

Twitter Sentiment Assessment (TSA) has become a critical area of study in recent years, gaining significant attention due to the widespread use of social media platforms like Twitter for sharing opinions on products and services. This shift has complicate traditional survey methods, making social platform mining a preferred alternative for gathering user feedback. However, the unstructured nature of these posts presents challenges in automatically classifying user sentiments. This paper presents an automated system for analyzing Twitter sentiment by leveraging Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) frameworks. TSA was conducted using two distinct datasets: one English set and one Hindi set. Results demonstrated an accuracy of 82.2% for Twitter Sentiment Assessment in the English language and 75.4% for the Hindi language.

Conventional dialogue systems are typically restricted to constricted, constrained question-answer sets, whereas contemporary large pre-trained language models have demonstrated the ability to generate coherent conversations within confined contexts. This disparity motivates our introduction of DLTL, an extensive person-centric (specifically Li Li, modeled after real humans) framework designed for domains with limited scope, allowing for unbounded conversation generation within a specific role. The primary objective is to determine the optimal pre-trained language model architecture and the ideal post-training strategy to maximize human likeness in conversational output. Specifically, our study investigates the use of non-role or character-focused approaches versus role-specific architectures, evaluating training methods that range from fine-tuning to supervised conversational pre-training. Empirical results indicate that a model employing both pre-training strategies excels in simulating authentic interactions. Furthermore, effective integration of both approaches yields the most favorable outcomes.

"Remembrance" refers to a mechanism by which a black hole acquires and retains additional mass from environmental particles or surrounding waves, occurring independently of Hawking radiation. This phenomenon, applicable to both isolated and merging black holes, causes their final masses to be environment-dependent. Consequently, a population of black holes could generate a widespread gravitational wave background, characterized by waves that are both Gaussian and random in nature. This stochastic backdrop arises because the specific environmental influence on a black hole's growth varies randomly. Distinguishing this signal from standard stochastic backgrounds produced by unresolved binary mergers is possible; the two signatures differ in their red evolution, an attribute termed "redness." Moreover, this signal could be detected before standard stochastic signals, offering the potential for detection within the LISA frequency band.

We examine a model based on a singlet chiral superfield that transmits the gravitational interaction between trees. This framework postulates a spontaneous breaking of supersymmetry via a shift in energy scale, mediated by a heavy scalar. The resulting energy scale and mass of the mediator are determined by the vacuum expectation value of a complex parameter characterized by both magnitude and direction. We analyze the dynamics of this parameter's real and imaginary components, treating the scenario where they acquire vacuum expectation values as distinct phases of symmetry breaking. The transition from where the field's components possess negligible vacuum expectation values to where they acquire non-zero values is shown to be a second-order phase transition, yielding observable consequences in three parts. First, the model provides mechanisms to explain the bathe scale splitting of quarks. Second, it offers sources for a detectable spectrum of gravitational waves. Third, it enables the formation of stable exotic objects known as dark matter black holes formed during the early universe.

This research introduces an innovative architecture for training signaling games through the integration of neuro-symbiosisic causal inference (NSCI). The training framework relies on a structured data format comprising three core elements: (1) a high-level symbolic description of the task environment, (2) the probability distributions for generating states and actions, and (3) a high-level explanation for the underlying reward mechanism. The network utilizes the symbolic information to construct a causal model, which drives the learning of optimal low-level decision rules aligned with that explanation. These emerging capabilities for abstract reasoning and the generation of value-based signaling facilitate efficient knowledge transfer to agents operating in base tasks, as well as rapid adaptation to new variations of those tasks. Experimental results highlight the system's dual capacity: the symbolics not only produce interpretable high-fidelity strategies but also enable the formation of semantic signals that support effective learning in the agent's baseline scenarios and fast acquisition of new reward structures.

Forecasting specific vocabulary terms is a critical task with broad applications in various domains. For example, identifying emerging search terms assists e-commerce firms with inventory planning, while tracking new technical terminology enables software developers to update documentation and maintain current technology stacks. Despite these advantages, no current system effectively predicts term usage with flexibility, efficiency, and accuracy simultaneously. Addressing this gap, we introduce a hybrid framework for term prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques application-wise, yielding more accurate predictions with greater flexibility and efficiency.

We present the use-phase suggestion system driven by two-phase session model that demonstrates improved performance on online A/B experiments within a e-commerce environment. Leveraging a data-centric approach for mining session information from user history, the suggested items are obtained by combining fully-unsupervised clustering with supervised learning. In addition, the relative rankings of the candidate items are regulated by a new vector representation model that captures both session and product attributes via a latent variable method. Empirical results on a real-world dataset indicate that our proposed algorithm outperforms baseline techniques in predicting session items and accurately ranking the priority of the recommended items with higher dimensional features.

The behavior of passive colloids moving within a bath of active particles is significantly influenced by system-scale forces. While earlier research successfully modeled this effect in equilibrium colloidal environments, it has recently been extended to contexts lacking equilibrium conditions. Models incorporating effective system-scale forces have been developed, while experiments have demonstrated how active particles drive non-equilibrium processes at larger scales, creating effective "currents" that displace non-active components. However, a key limitation remains: earlier models rely heavily on specific assumptions and their derived effects are typically valid only within low-density limits for non-active particles. In contrast, we present a novel theoretical framework based on a coarse-grained view of momentum conservation that remains accurate regardless of the concentration density, removing previous model-specific equilibrium constraints. We demonstrate how directional currents formed by non-active particles depend on their spatial arrangement and their individual run-and-tumble characteristics. Furthermore, our analysis reveals effective forces acting on non-active particles that can be substantially stronger than those predicted in equilibrium-based theories at non-equilibrium steady states, and we explore the physical mechanisms underlying this anomaly.

We present a novel numerical framework for analyzing fluid transport within complex discretized models of discrete fractures. The approach decomposes a discretization of a three-dimensional domain into a hierarchy of structured grids: unstructured grids representing individual fractures and two grids for every two-dimensional plane, ensuring their collective union forms a conformant, dimensionally varying network. On these grids, a Mimetic Finite Difference scheme is applied to derive a conservative discretization of the div($D(x, D_{ij})$grad($P$)) equation, accounting for the fracture network's anisotropic, degenerate diffusion tensor. Here, $P$ denotes the fluid's pressure, $D_{ij}$ is the diffusivity, and the integration path varies based on the local dimension. The approach is conservative, and the system of linear equations is solved efficiently. The approach is shown to be consistent with the continuum formulation, and numerical tests are provided to demonstrate its accuracy and high performance.

This study addresses two key issues in drone swarms: maintaining cellular structure and avoiding collisions. We introduce new methods based on minimizing the alignment of point set centroids. The first method, introduced here, maintains cell shape by ensuring points within each corresponding cell across all drones have aligned centroids. The paper reveals that this first approach more efficiently preserves cellular structure. However, as demonstrated by our analysis, neither strategy is sufficient to fully prevent collisions.

Optimal management models that account for dependencies among agents over time—specifically those influenced by delayed feedback and fractional noise—are formalized here as the optimal management solutions to a centralized problem of stochastic dynamics under delay (SSDF). This issue is first cast into an issue of parabolic equations under delay (SSDE), for which we present sufficient and necessary conditions that this issue exists. We then present some sufficient conditions for a problem of stochastic dynamics under delay (SSDD), showing its relationship to the issue mentioned earlier, before utilizing this issue to present a program for real-world applications that confirms the model's efficacy through an application to a financial context.

This study investigates the spectral characteristics within a non-self-adjoint Dirac operator containing bounded, periodic potentials. Our findings reveal a continuum spectrum bounded by two rings of isolated eigenvalues; by applying boundary conditions that render the spectrum purely discrete, we establish existence and oscillation properties of these eigenvalues. Furthermore, by utilizing the associated elliptity structure, we demonstrate that these eigenvalues can be organized using generalized Poincaré polynomials derived from abelian extensions of x-additive rings. Our work parallels recent research by B. yon Sz. Nathansen on energy levels imposed on quantum mechanical systems of similar nature through his recent research. However, our approach diverges significantly due to the non-Hermitian nature of our operator, thereby extending these concepts into a new analytical framework for periodic operators without gap structures but rich internal spectral topology.

This paper proposes a novel architecture for heterogeneous vehicle networks, designed to ensure robust and seamless connectivity. Divided into a lower tier and an upper tier, this framework enables direct vehicle-to-roadside unit (RSU) links in the first tier for primary data transmission, while the second tier offers a supplementary layer of communication through relays on moving vehicles. The study begins by constructing a stochastic geometry-based model of the network and deriving the probability density functions (PDFs) for both tiers. To validate these findings, Monte-Carlo simulations are employed, which also allow for the analytical results, demonstrating their high accuracy. Leveraging the derived PDFs, the authors calculate key performance indicators—including signal-to-interference-and-noise ratio (SIR) distributions, packet error rates (PER), and average transmission rates. Ultimately, the paper investigates various factors influencing first-tier communications, with particular emphasis on analyzing the SIR distributions and the resulting packet error rates across both network tiers to substantiate the practicality of this two-tier structure, supported by simulation data.

Although Wikipedia serves as a highly reliable online encyclopedia where users can continually enhance its content, some articles contain inaccuracies. To mitigate this, we investigated the utility of analyzing edit patterns for identifying submissions of low quality. We proposed methods that analyze the sequences of user editing actions to detect poor materials, findings show that this approach outperforms standard methods relying solely on utility metrics like page views and image ratings. We developed two additional approaches: one marks an article as low quality if a single user makes numerous edits to it, while the other identifies certain persistent editing patterns associated with subpar content. We evaluated our methods using our newly compiled dataset, which records both the categories of edit contributions and article quality levels.

This study addresses knowledge transfer in continuous control problems where a decision-making agent must be trained using access to a learnable model. Unlike traditional settings, learning occurs through an opaque black-box interface that reveals only state rewards, obscuring the underlying environment dynamics. We introduce a method to train a replayable world model by estimating the latent linear Gaussian dynamical structure from black-box trajectories. This approach relies on the assumption that the prior dynamics follow linear-Gaussian distributions, which enables the explicit modeling of unobserved state transitions by inferring and integrating out these latent variables. By providing a trained approximate of the latent dynamics to the learner, we demonstrate that this trained black-box agent can achieve near-optimal performance. Our findings show that learned agents perform at comparable levels to those trained with full state visibility. Additionally, we establish a theoretical bound on the generalization error of the learners' policies derived from this black-box framework.

This study details the initial observation of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay, along with evidence suggesting the presence of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$, derived from an analysis of $1.8\times10^9$ $b$-hadron collisions recorded by the LHCb experiment at center-of-mass energies corresponding to $\sqrt{s}=7$ and $8$ TeV. The measured branching fraction for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ is $0.92\pm0.16\pm0.17$ times $10^{-3}$, with an evidence level exceeding $5\sigma$. Furthermore, the mass distribution profile for the $D^0 K^0_S$ system exhibits an excess beyond $4\sigma$ near the $D^0 K^0_{S1}^*$ mass.

This research extends the local geometric description of T-duality from the work of Hori and Rocek [1] to include topologically nontrified twisted tori over three-dimensional $U(1)$-principal bundles over a torus. This generalization employs the language of $B$-field gerbes and demonstrates both the gauge symmetry within the $B$-gerbe framework and global T-duality arising from exchanging base-space $U(1)$-bundles with dual ones. A key outcome is a rigorous derivation of the $E_7$ symmetry observed in abelian T-dualities of torus backgrounds, as previously noted in Horowitz's work [3]. Additionally, a Riemann-Hurwitz-type formula characterizing the variation in Betti numbers under T-duality is developed.

Current observance methods, such as imitation learning, often fail to generalize well because they are limited by the constraints of the training environment and the quality of the teacher's actions. To address this, we present Co-OIiL (Joint Observation-Information Learning), a novel framework designed to boost the sample efficiency and robustness of policy learning under limited, low-variance demonstration data. Our approach jointly models the dynamics of both the demonstration and real target systems while correcting for distributional shifts via importance weighting based on joint observational likelihood. By employing variational inference, we achieve flexible, non-parametric adaptation of these dynamics to underlying latent variables without requiring specialized expert demonstrations. Extensive experiments on two real-world robotic manipulation tasks confirm that the effectiveness of our method, in particular, its ability to transfer policies across different simulation-to-reality contexts, is statistically significant.

Cyclic codes represent a key category of linear error-correcting methods, valued for their ease of implementation and reliability. Historically, however, no member of this family achieved performance rivaling that of modern codes. Recent research has reintroduced interest in cyclic codes through the discovery of Periodic Anisotropy (PAC) codes, a previously underappreciated subclass that now offers competitive capabilities. Unfortunately, applying PAC codes demands knowledge of specific parameters, which are currently determined via exhaustive search. To address this bottleneck, this research proposes two computational methods for determining these parameters. The work also empirically evaluates the performance of previously unp measured PAC codes, revealing that certain code combinations provide outstanding results and could surpass the industry standard, which remains dominated by LDPC codes.

Hand interactions with objects are vital for executing complex tasks, yet current capture and recovery methods are limited by the need for specialized equipment, controlled settings, and data series that lack hands or involve empty objects. This paper introduces a solution using an RGB-D camera to monitor hands and simultaneously build representations of objects in real-time. Our system automatically reconstructs the virtual hands and physical objects from a sequence of point clouds, allowing the prediction of future point cloud series based on these models. Consequently, we can track object interactions, classify them into known categories, and ultimately recover models of how hands engage with objects during natural object manipulation. This paper presents the corresponding algorithms and datasets to support these advancements.

This paper proposes a treatment disruption model designed to capture contextual interference. Specifically, it investigates how exposure to a treatment group varies according to proximity to a treated unit, utilizing a kernel function that diminishes with distance. Similarly, it considers a kernel function applicable to outcomes that also attenuates over distance. Using these principles, we develop a treatment disruption metric to identify whether specific units exhibit patterns consistent with contextual interference. This metric evaluates the extent to which a unit's actual outcome deviates from its K-nearest neighbor composite outcome for units in the control condition.

Next, we analyze the distributional characteristics of this metric and establish a testing procedure to determine if contextual interference is present. Simulation studies demonstrate that the resulting test achieves high statistical power in detecting contextual interference and maintains accurate type-I error rates. Finally, we apply the metric and associated test to identify treatment disruption in data concerning summer employment opportunities and subsequent wage growth among teenagers.

We introduce a new, high-density-dependent contribution to neutrino emission during Dark Matter (DM) annihilation within astrophysical objects, occurring via a four-body process involving two pseudoscalar DM particles and two neutrinos. Calculating the emission rate demands solving the Euler-Lagrange equations for produced neutrinos, which necessitates knowledge of the local density profiles for both dark and visible matter. This rigorous high-density framework enables a more accurate determination of the neutrino energy distribution at Earth, facilitating refined constraints on the pseudoscalar DM-nucleon interaction cross-section.

This dual-band architecture successfully accommodates the scissors transition in $O(5)$-adverse scenarios. We illustrate these phenomena with case studies of an Mn-O-Mn octahedral framework within an MnO$_2$ monolayer, specifically looking at $e_g$ and $t_{2g}$ orbitals. Finally, we outline the potential for such controlled manipulation of orbital states and electronic properties to enable novel device functionalities in oxides that terminate in monatomic oxygen-rich or hydroxyl surfaces.

Achieing ultra-low temperatures is a crucial initial phase for contemporary and emerging optical technologies, such as quantum simulation and optical quantum computing. It is often puzzling how models like CNNs and RNNs learn relatively straightforward feature representations despite solving complex tasks, often requiring high neural network complexity as a price. Modern data-driven and randomized modeling methods, including Bayesian and frequentist inference, machine learning, and optimization, are widely used for their superior statistical accuracy and computational efficiency. Conversely, they often overlook deep domain knowledge, which can lead to unrealistic assumptions and reduced effectiveness. Although traditional modeling integrates domain insights, it is typically rigid and requires extensive manual adjustment. To address these challenges, this paper introduces "collaborative data-informed modeling" (CIM), a new framework that integrates both contemporary learning algorithms and expert domain knowledge into statistical and optimization procedures. By updating algorithm parameters—specifically those for loss functions and priors—through iterative interactions with domain experts, CIM operates with a "two-step cycling" process. This approach allows pure reliance on data and expert-driven insights to reinforce one another. The method's implementation and theoretical properties are examined for two key machine learning applications: supervised reinforcement and unsupervised representation. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate how successfully CIM bridges the gap between statistical accuracy and practical feasibility by incorporating domain expertise alongside statistical data.

This study examines the performance of degree-degree linked LDPC codes (dd-LDPC) on binary erasure channels. By applying a mean-field approach, we derive an equation for the expected erasure ratio as a function of the channel's erasure probability and the network's joint degree distribution. Because solving this expression for the steady-state erasure ratio is analytically intractable, we instead employ two complementary strategies to evaluate performance: first, leveraging numerical techniques, particularly bifurcation theory, to determine optimal joint degree distributions for achieving a target erasure rate; second, utilizing a new proposed lower bound for steady-state errors to identify best-performance dd-LDPC structures efficiently. Our findings, illustrated with examples of bipartite matching and cyclic quaternary cyclic shift-matching networks, confirm the efficacy of our analysis and highlight a particularly promising class of codes featuring balanced high-degree nodes distributed uniformly across different amplitude levels.

Safety filters are designed to ensure that the output of control systems remains within defined safe boundaries. Conventional filtering methods often compromise filtering performance in an attempt to maintain safety, or they incur additional computational costs to guarantee it. To mitigate these drawbacks, this work introduces the prognostic safety filter (PSF), which leverages system realization from the $H_\infty$ control framework to maintain safety while preserving control performance. The system is represented as a switched linear model where the switching sequence corresponds to the discrete mode switch, and the realization output is constructed as a linear blend of the individual switching subsystem outputs, with weights derived to satisfy specific constraints. The proposed solution ensures safety by maintaining the control output within a defined safe set, even in the event of sensor failures. The resulting optimization problem is formulated with decision variables that remain continuous throughout most stages, except for specific variables that are constrained to be non-negative.

This study introduces a new approach to building speech synthesis models for previously unrecordled languages by utilizing transcript annotations derived from Elicited Language Eliciation (ELE) studies. This study investigates the dynamical interaction between jets and outflows around young stars using 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations. Basket studies allow for simultaneous assessments of a treatment's efficacy across multiple similar indications, governed by designs that may be basket-wide uniform or customized per site. We illustrate the application of our design and estimation method using data from a simulated two-stage basket trial focused on small oncology tumors.

Pre-training using self-supervised methods has proven highly effective for enhancing performance on labeled tasks. Current approaches are largely supervised, depending on reliable labels such as fine-grained annotations for contrastive learning or identity labels for instance discrimination. However, in practical settings, not all training data possesses this fine-grined label availability, as seen in modalities like audio, where such detailed markings are labor-intensive, or medical images, where data is scarce. To address this, we introduce PILoC, a framework designed to handle such cases by partitioning unlabeled instances into cyclic generator-discriminator pairs. This method leverages the presence of well-labeled modalities to create initial partitions and then extends the learning to unlabeled domains through a specialized loss function that enforces consistency with the labeled learning patterns. Our comprehensive evaluations across multiple modalities confirm that PILoC successfully captures pre-training signals from labeled sources and correctly identifies structural patterns within labeled data, ultimately yielding significant performance boosts on top-down tasks across various domains.

The proposed FM-RSTM structure was validated through training on two standard temporal action prediction datasets, with the results demonstrating its superior performance in action prediction compared to both deep learning models and traditional machine learning methods.

This work demonstrates that maximal entanglement in a two-qubit system can be confirmed by violating the Bell inequality, despite the presence of experimental imperfections. "Flat bands" have recently become a focal point of research due to their association with highly unconventional states of matter, including quantum spin liquids and various forms of fractionalization, driven specifically by the flatness of these energy bands. However, this reasoning has driven paradoxical conclusions: since flat bands imply infinite quasiparticle masses and consequently zero speed, they suggest that electrons are entirely confined to loop paths and cannot move between them. This article challenges the standard interpretation by demonstrating that truly flat bands inherently possess non-zero, albeit minimal, energy dispersion and quasicarrier velocities, rather than being strictly featureless. We establish that even slight deviations from flatness allow electrons to transition from one flat band to adjacent ones, effectively terminating the confinement assumed in previous models.

To support correct automatic differentiation, backpropagation must traverse every operator while carefully accumulating gradients according to the specific path of the forward pass. This process traditionally involves sequentially executing backpropagation steps across all layers, which incurs overhead. We introduce a technique that dynamically executes backpropagation in the inverse order of the forward pass, dynamically organizes execution based on computational subgraphs, and efficiently skips redundant operations by leveraging forward execution history.

This study presents an automotive control architecture designed to switch seamlessly between autonomous and manual driving modes, effectively serving as fail-safe mechanism. Architecturally, it integrates three primary components: a decision unit that monitors transition conditions, distinct control engines tailored for each mode, and a filtering stage to ensure continuity at mode switches. Utilizing Occam process networks for mathematical modeling, this work performs formal verification based on two critical requirements: first, that each mode's control policy is executed following a respective trigger, and second, that pre- and post-condition constraints are maintained during switch transitions to prevent state inconsistency. By employing formal methods, we demonstrate that this architecture successfully enforces safety under these conditions.

Although intensity fluctuation measurements at neutral hydrogen (HI) frequencies offer significant potential for probing the large-scale structure of the universe, current interferometric arrays face limitations imposed by various disturbance sources. This study examines how observed data, which inherently contain disturbances from out-of-field observations, impact HI intensity mapping. We present simulations that evaluate a widely used background subtraction technique and demonstrate that, while observations are typically contaminated by a background noise level exceeding the signal by over an order of magnitude, the specific disturbances remain statistically negligible up to large angular scales. Our analysis reveals that the characteristic power spectrum is suppressed by a factor of approximately 100 due of dominant foreground excess, whereas the disturbances themselves reduce the detectable signal strength by roughly 1/80 across all scales. Although the observed data are primarily governed by the foreground-boosted background noise, the contribution from disturbance noise becomes comparable at scales smaller than the angular scale ($k < 0.4$ h Mpc$^{-4}$). Although we acknowledge that specific disturbances vary by telescope design, the findings suggest that future HI intensity mapping experiments will largely remain noise-limited rather than being constrained by disturbance limits.

Recent advancements in Big Data and Machine Learning have fueled significant growth in e-commerce platforms, which, however, have simultaneously intensified competition. A primary challenge for these platforms is providing users with a continuously refined list of personalized product suggestions. While traditional collaborative filtering and context-aware approaches often rely on a blend of textual data (reviews, specifications) and numerical data (ratings, clicks) to build models, this paper proposes focusing exclusively on harnessing contextual information derived solely from user-generated product reviews. By employing context-aware techniques, the study extracts latent attributes from reviews and analyzes user behavior within various product context spaces to establish a hybrid collaborative model. Furthermore, the research introduces a hybrid recommendation method that integrates pattern-based collaborative filtering with content-aware strategies. Leveraging specific data mining algorithms, the proposal framework merges content-aware and pattern-based methods to uniquely suggest new items to purchasers. This hybrid approach aims to enhance recommendation accuracy, user engagement, and overall satisfaction. We utilized the Amazon Video Game dataset for validation and benchmarked our method against state-of-the-art collaborative, filtering, and content-aware algorithms. Our results indicate that the proposed solution outperforms these existing techniques in precision, recall, and the accuracy of rank-ordered lists.

This study introduces the concept of parity-symmetry-protected bundle emission, where a collection of any even number of Majorana zero modes (MZMs) arises at the corners of a two-dimensional topological insulator insulated by a $\nu = 1$ Chern insulator. By terminating this insulator with heterojunctions between $s$-wave and d-wave superconductors, the system's gap can be tuned to generate the mentioned corner MZBs. The operation relies on the parity symmetry inherent to the topological corner modes within these insulators, ensuring their stability. While bundle emission cannot be controlled by simply shifting chemical potential or applying external magnetic fields, its regulation is achieved by inducing a phase transition to an anisotropic $d+id$ superconducting state through specific superconducting phase differences. This configuration offers a promising pathway for generating and managing Majorana corner modes within compact two-dimensional topological circuits for quantum computing applications.

This study introduces a novel, precise, and exact analytical formulation for the equation of state of non-degenerate non-relativistic ideal alkali gases in thermal equilibrium. By analytically deriving expressions for pressure, specific heat, adiabatic exponent, and enthalpy as functions of density and temperature, we enable closed-form calculations for these properties. These capabilities allow for the derivation of accurate analytical descriptions for alkali gases existing in various states of local thermal equilibrium, including scenarios involving time-dependent pressure and temperature. When in local equilibrium, even when the slowest-varying spatial derivative scales as $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^2)$ where $\epsilon = \lambda/L$ represents the ratio of the wavelength to the characteristic length, the resulting dynamic equations for the first two $\epsilon$-orders reduce to the well-known acoustic and Euler systems of hydrodynamics, respectively. Furthermore, our findings for isentropic pressure expansions are applied to model shock waves in alkali gases, yielding accurate predictions for the resulting shock polar and subsequent velocity C-jump conditions across the shock front.

This study investigates the properties of vector mesons within an environment exhibiting momentum-dependent vacuum particle production and mirror symmetry violation. Calculations were performed employing the constituent quark model in combination with the Hartree-Phenomenological Functional (HRT) approximation. Modeling the non-constant medium as chiral-imbalanced terrain, we identified that the physical masses of these states correspond to the real component of the constituent quark propagator's diagonal element at a specific diagonal matrix value. Our results indicate a shifting spectrum where both light and heavy vector mesons tend towards lower physical mass values under medium conditions compared to their vacuum states, consistently decreasing with enhanced medium density and chiral asymmetry. Additionally, the present analysis suggests that the constituent quark chemical potential can be accurately approximated by the medium's actual particle chemical potential.

This paper addresses the problem of estimating average degree and clustering coefficients in an unknown network where a fraction of nodes are compromised by an adversary capable of returning arbitrary values for these metrics from selected nodes. We further examine the performance and application of these methods on small-world graphs, supported by numerical results that confirm their efficacy in accurately estimating parameters within such networks despite the presence of adversarial nodes.

Knowledge distillation has proven to be an efficient strategy for deploying large models in resource-limited environments. In the realm of multiple-instructor distillation, previous approaches have struggled because they simply average the outputs of multiple teachers, often causing teachers to conflict and causing valuable teacher signals to be lost. This paper introduces Pairwise Iterative Logits Coalition (PILE), an optimization approach for multi-instructor knowledge distillation. PILE avoids the output stage entirely and instead aligns the teachers' logits directly. Our method iteratively pairs teachers at the feature level to promote their cooperation over typical output-based methods. Additionally, our model iteratively adjusts the combination weights of the teachers based on their features, ensuring that informative signals are captured while suppressing those that are uninformative or contradictory. Experiments on various object detection and segmentation tasks demonstrate that our framework outperforms existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art results.

By minimizing the $H^1$-semi-norm of functions outside $\Omega$ subject to their trace on $\Omega$ matching a given data function $f$ on the boundary, the problem effectively seeks the most compact representation possible under these constraints. We prove that for any $f \in L^2(\Gamma)$, this formulation yields at least one solution; moreover, if the mean value of $f$ is zero, the resulting norm of the minimizer is the lowest achievable. The paper further analyzes how the mean component of $f$ influences the solution and its properties. Uniqueness is established in specific scenarios, notably involving the representation of signed measures. We demonstrate that if a signed Borel measure $f$ on $\Gamma$ is represented minimally by a function with compact support in $\Omega$ (assuming $n=3$), then the representation is unique iff the measure has no components orthogonal to the normal vector of $\Gamma$. Additionally, we show that if $f$ is a sum of Dirac deltas at distinct points on $\Gamma$, the corresponding representation by a function with compact support in $\Omega$ is also unique.

Match-dependent table operations have emerged as a critical P4 capability, allowing the runtime to control what depends on incoming packets regarding which action groups are executed. Although standard implementations typically utilize fixed-length stacks ranked by match-table priority, utilizing linked lists offers an advantage by dynamically allocating memory based on packet headers, thus conserving buffer space. To enable developers to easily program this high-efficiency scenario, our P16 open-source compiler extends the Match-Table feature to function with both fixed-length stacks and variable-length structures (specifically fixed or free-forming item lists). Our test results confirm that this approach not only saves packet buffer space but also enhances the performance of actions with a higher volume of data processing compared to the P11 standard. Our P11 compiler is accessible at the repository: https://github.com/CSE-UPB/p11-compiler.

The paper examines the precision of vector-benchtop (VBFEM) discretisations for the surface-transport (ST) equation, which characterizes sediment movement in open channels in its steady-state form. These elements, when combined with the Debris-Flow Model (DFM), are capable of accurately predicting both the sediment transport rate and channel evolution over time, based on their ability to handle these specific problems. However, despite these advantages, it has been observed that the overall accuracy of these solutions is restricted by the choice of numerical fluxes, particularly those employed for estimating the advective term. In this paper we demonstrate that a newly developed flux function enhances accuracy significantly, and we quantify this improvement through an analysis of numerical experiments involving both uniform and non-uniform sediment transport rate scenarios, as well as channels with varying geometries.

Federated Learning (FL) stands as a prominent decentralized machine learning approach that safeguards user privacy by preventing the sharing of training datasets. However, numerous FL systems inadvertently expose sensitive information indirectly through the exchange of model parameters, often without adequate assessment or mitigation of such leakage. While previous FL research has largely relied on Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) to protect sensitive labels, we demonstrate that SDG methods inadvertently expose them during the data synthesis process. To address this gap, we introduce the Differential Confidentiality in FL (DCFL) framework, which establishes the first mechanism ensuring differential privacy across distributed data environments. Our analysis reveals the trade-off between privacy and the accuracy of model parameters, allowing system designers to selectively adjust the privacy level of specific features. Consequently, DCFL enables flexible strategies to either render sensitive data completely inaccessible or maintain access while ensuring a fully quantified and controlled privacy guarantee.

We introduce an Runge-Kutta continuous-phase formulation that enables the continuous computation of solution trajectories, stage values, and numerical coefficients. This formulation has been integrated into a Runge-Kutta continuous-phase estimator designed for solving ordinary differential equations. An explicit estimator of error is also developed. Furthermore, we present a method for determining the optimal coefficients of Runge-Kutta schemes using the continuous phase approach combined with an algorithm for generating optimal linear estimators, derived via the continuous phase continuous stage values.

The computational demands for training large-scale neural networks have historically necessitated expensive, specialized hardware. Consequently, the costs associated with prototyping new models remain prohibitive, and current architectures are constrained by available hardware resources. As models continue to expand in size, the requirement for additional compute power grows at an accelerated rate. Addressing this, we propose an efficient framework for model-parallel training of neural networks that eliminates the need for extra hardware by utilizing existing resources more effectively. By partitioning and distributing the compute units across a system, we enable the scaling of architectures that was previously unattainable on a singular processor. Furthermore, we present the first application of this technique to Gated Computation Networks (GCNs). In experiments, this approach reduced the physical memory footprint by a factor of four and enhanced training speed on a twelve-billion parameter model, thereby demonstrating the most rapid training to date for any processor of comparable scale.

This study investigates chaotic scattering within the dissipative Heisenberg spin map, a system that has drawn significant interest in both physics and mathematics. We focus on the Wada basin phenomenon, where boundaries separating basins of attraction share the same topological properties due to mutual co-boundary status, first identified by Wada in 1982. Our results demonstrate that minimal energy loss generates Wada boundaries across the entire basins of attraction for three coexisting transient chaotat states—previously unobserved in such contexts. Furthermore, dissipation stabilizes these boundary structures and dramatically expands the attractable volume of the non-attracting chaotat states. Volume expansion of up to 98% was recorded, drastically reducing initial conditions required for chaos and shortening time-series lengths needed to establish convergence significantly. Additionally, we identified that the unstable periodic orbits constituting the skeleton of these non-attracting chaotat states are all weakly perturbationally stable under dissipative conditions, a finding at odds with traditional non-attracting behavior. Collectively, these insights offer fresh perspectives on the origins and characteristics of Wada sets as they pertain to transient chaos and dissipation.

While recent research has demonstrated that an electric dipole-moment (EDM) axletone can be detected by "taste-changing" monitors (blind people whose natural loss of taste is restored), such a system is limited because the effect fades quickly once the lab environment is altered. In fact, a similar system could be constructed using an electric diplet-moment (Elettlet) photonlet, which changes smell rather than taste. However, unlike the previous system, this new setup might have some unexpected durability because the effect does not stop when the laboratory environment is changed again. Activity recognition in clips is essential for analyzing short sequences of video, which is widely used in surveillance, monitoring, and monitoring. Addressing this challenge is difficult because activity patterns vary based on the performed action, the actors' positions, the scene, the timing, and the duration of clips. Existing methods are constrained by architecture, input size, or training data limitations. To overcome these barriers, this paper presents a new network architecture, Hierarchical Focus (HFNet), which optimizes feature extraction from clips. HFNet is founded on a novel hierarchical focus mechanism: it hierarchically and adaptively selects informative regions from clips, identifies activity cues within those regions, and aggregates the resulting features. Additionally, the paper describes a novel approach for augmenting input video. This augmentation technique improves HFNet's robustness to actors' poses, positions, timing variations, and clip length. Experimental results demonstrate that HFNet, augmented as suggested, surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches in accuracy. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengzheng1991/HHFNet/.

This study explores the stability of the thermodynamic equilibrium for the Reissner-Nordström-anti-de Sitter (RNSAdS) black hole while incorporating electromin induced scalar self-interaction within scalar field theory. By applying the first law of thermodynamics alongside specific variations in Einstein's gravity framework, specific conditions for heat stability are derived and examined under different self-interaction strength scenarios. The results show an exponential behavior for the specific heat near critical points, governed by a derivative of the square root of the potential function related to the scalar field. The analysis indicates that RNSAdS black holes maintain thermodynamic equilibrium only when examining specific self-interaction regimes. Furthermore, the results show that a test charged particle can successfully fall into these stable black holes without violating cosmic censorship, provided the particle meets certain mass constraints.

Stellar birth is a complex, multi-stage process driven by gravity within the cold molecular clouds of intermolecular space. These structures, which can span hundreds of light-years and contain millions of stars, are primarily made of molecular hydrogen. As denser regions within these clouds begin to contract under gravitational forces, individual stars begin to form. When a star eventually reaches the main sequence, it enters a stable phase determined by its specific mass.

This work demonstrates that nested sampling serves as an effective method for calculating various forms of entropy, including Gibbs-Shannon, Renyi, and Tsallis entropies. These quantities are vital for characterizing the degree of uniformity within a probability distribution. The study establishes that the fundamental dynamic of nested sampling, namely the uniform sampling of prior density contours, yields direct estimates for these entropy metrics. When governed by specific parameters, the Renyi and Tsallis entropies reduce to the Gibbs-Shannon form; thus, we present a systematic approach for computing all four types. The utility and accuracy of these estimators were validated through two standard benchmarks: Monte Carlo simulations of the Ising model and experiments on quantum states prepared and analyzed via a quantum computing platform. The results demonstrate high computational accuracy.

We analyze the measure-valued convergence of both the finite volume methods with piecewise-constant approximations applied to a specific hyperbolic conservation law. This law follows a "Riemann problem" setup and aligns with equation (1). It is noted that this law corresponds to a specific case where solutions may not be conservative in the standard sense, thus precluding easy analysis using entropy methods. Despite this challenge, we demonstrate that these numerical solutions converge weakly to a measure-valued center of a specific type, assuming the initial data is of bounded variation. Our result aligns with previous theoretical expectations.

In recent years, Internet of Things (IoT) devices have experienced rapid growth, providing a wide array of services and applications. However, this expansion has concurrently increased exposure to assault. While current state-of-the-attack solutions often employ sophisticated techniques like Deep Learning, these methods typically demand high computational resources, rendering them incompatible with IoT environments due to constraints in processing power and memory. Furthermore, existing systems frequently fail to utilize available local resources efficiently. To address these challenges, this paper proposes "NB coded," a lightweight classification framework designed for IoT devices. This system leverages the native capabilities of 802.15.4 wireless networks and optimizes classification through a model built on encoded features derived from a Naïve Bayes classifier. Experimental results demonstrate that the system achieves classification accuracy of 98.05% while maintaining minimal memory and power footprints, thus meeting specific IoT limitations.

The broad class of integrable evolution equations known as nonlinear wave equations (NWEs) includes prominent models such as the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation and the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation. A central feature shared by these integrable systems is their ability to linearize under specific transformations, thereby establishing a correspondence between solutions of the NWEs and those of linear equations (LEs). Specifically, this paper investigates the inverse scattering relationship between solutions of the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equation and those of two distinct linear problems: the one-dimensional wave equation (1D-WE) and a variant called charged wave equation (CWE). It demonstrates that while both linearizations can generate exact solutions for the KPZ, this approach fails to fully resolve the problem due to technical constraints, particularly regarding unbounded solutions. By introducing the reverse scattering method within an integrable formulation for the wave-bogoliubov (W-B) and charged wave-equation (CWE)-KPZ mappings, this paper overcomes these limitations while offering a unified perspective on integrable NWEs via the lens of linear theory. Furthermore, it provides a novel explanation for the noise mechanism inherent in integrable versions of these equations, significantly advancing the understanding of stochastic NWEs by emphasizing the importance of the linearization transformation in this field.

During the MMS mission's survey of the solar wind, several events were recorded where Alfvénic fluctuations exhibited spectral breaks occurring at frequencies matching ion cyclotron frequencies ($f_{ci}$). These findings offer the earliest space-based confirmation of compressive turbulence operating at compressive scales smaller than the ion gyro-radius, a regime theoretically predicted to exist once the ion cascade transcends a kinetic spectral break.

These outcomes demonstrate that a time-comb of isolated electronic pulses can be synthesized from a standard femtosecond laser source. This novel methodology offers significant utility for time-resolved experiments, enabling the observation and manipulation of nonlinear optical effects.

This analysis investigates alternative mechanisms, specifically tidal disruption, accretion, and magnetic dynamo activity, to explain the mid-infrared flare. Drawing upon theoretical models, we estimate a mass range of 0.005–0.02 solar Earths for the disrupted object. Ultimately, the phenomenon is concluded to result from a combination of tidal disruption and accretion, with the subsequent mid-infrared emission attributed to kinetic-to-radiative energy conversion driven by accretion and the subsequent release of gravitational binding energy.

Measurements of inclusive cross sections for pions, kaons, (anti-)protons, and $\phi$ mesons are reported for central collisions of xenon on xenon at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.44$ TeV, utilizing data from the ALICE experiment at the LHC. The measurements cover rapidity intervals of $y \in [-0.5, 0.35]$ and $y \in [-3.0, -4.0]$. Analysis focuses primarily on transverse mass ranges of $m_{\rm T} \lesssim 2.5$ GeV/$c^2$ for $p$, $\bar{p}$, K$^\pm$, and neutral or charged K mesons ($K^\pm$), as well as $m_{\rm T} \lesssim 2.5$ GeV/$c^2$ for pions, with an extended range of $m_{\rm T} \lesssim 4.5$ GeV/$c^2$ available for $\pi^\pm$ and specific conditions for the $\phi$ meson. All results are presented as normalized yield per cross section as a function of transverse mass, subsequently compared against predictions from various phenomenological models, as well as archival ALICE measurements of these species in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 4$ and 5

Parton distribution functions (PDFs) are a fundamental component of many predictions made by the hadronic structure of nuclear particles, which are essential tools in the field. These PDFs are parameterized and determined through the fitting process, which involves a vast amount of experimental and theoretical data. Consequently, this study examines the interpolation and progression methods employed in PDFs. We demonstrate that employing effective approaches for both interpolation and progression can significantly reduce uncertainties associated with PDFs. Furthermore, this methodology proves that certain parameters included in the fitting process may be superfluous.

Sintered soil samples, such as those created using heat applied through radio frequency (RF) and microwaves, represent a promising solution for constructing habitats and returning to Mars. This study examines the impact of sintering temperatures on the mechanical behavior and microstructure of simulated lunar and Martian regoliths. Using cold press成型 samples with three distinct porosity levels (low, medium, and high), we subjected them to triaxial compression tests across temperature gradients from room temperature up to 1050°C. Results demonstrate that the yield stress and deviatoric strength of all soil types increase significantly with rising sintering temperatures. Additionally, micro-CT scanning revealed microstructural details, allowing us to quantify pore volume fraction, specific surface area, and pore size distribution. Analysis indicates that the specific surface area and smallest pore radius scale with the relative density of the samples, while the volume fraction of pores follows a quadratic relationship with relative density. Notably, the calculated yield stress from these models accurately matched experimental data across all temperature points and relative densities. Finally, the research evaluates the potential for creating self-healing regolith at specific thermal ranges to mitigate cracks and reduce structural failures in pressurized regolith reaction pressure vessels.

This research examines the Rayleigh-Plateau instability arising when a liquid film wrapped around a cylindrical fiber breaks up into droplets. The governing dynamics are captured by an inertial model that integrates both the hydrodynamics of the film in its coat-tail region and its motion as a bead on the fiber surface. By leveraging asymptotic analysis in the limit where the Fiber diameter is much smaller than the wavelength of perturbation, a set of eigenvalue problems is derived for each topological category characterized by an integer winding number \(n\), representing how many times the bead has wrapped the cylinder. Numerical solutions yield winding numbers \(n = 0, 1, 2\) with \(0 \leq \text{Im}(\omega) \leq 1\), revealing slip-enhanced breakup timescales and eigenfunctions for each mode. The study concludes by interpreting these results physically, emphasizing the role of slip in accelerating instability growth and outlining the conditions under which the asymptotic approximations remain valid.

The Star Formation Rate (SFR) is a fundamental parameter in astrophysics, yet the standard method for estimating it relies on photometric Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) fitting, which depends on assumptions about ionizing photon production, stellar evolution, dust properties, and mass distribution that remain controversial. This study offers a novel verification approach by utilizing the $\lambda$2165.9 $\rm{\AA}$ benchmark test originally proposed by Kennicutt (1998). This method compares the flux ratio of Brackett $\gamma$ ($\rm{Br}\gamma$) to Hydrogen $\delta$ ($\rm{H}\delta$) because the non-ionizing parts of these spectral lines are unaffected by dust extinction. By applying this test to 118 benchmark starburst galaxies analyzed in both the ZI (zero dust) and CIGALE (dust models) contexts, we find Br$\gamma$/Hd$\delta$ ratios from dust-free simulations align with observational data within 0.3 dex, confirming that current dust and SFR models are reliable. This agreement validates the accuracy of the predicted SFRs derived from these models.

The general diffusion model serves as a minimally biased, data-driven framework for characterizing time-evolving systems. Its broad applicability stems from requiring only two constraints: the existence of timescales significantly longer than its observational window and the presence of restricted restrictions limiting its parameters. This model has been deployed to analyze energy production and consumption patterns over the last century, resulting in three distinct phases: Phase I reflects pre-oil reliance, Phase II marks the industrial revolution triggered by oil dominance, and Phase III represents a potential sustainable shift driven by renewable energy adoption starting around 2008, assuming certain conditions hold true moving forward.

Recognizing handwritten documents is a critical task with extensive applications ranging from archiving ancient manuscripts and medical records to processing bank forms. While recent advancements in recognition technologies have largely concentrated on natural language text, handling the specialized symbols required in mathematical documents demands unique solutions due to distinct challenges. This study introduces an effective framework for identifying handwritten mathematics by fusing pen-based motion data with traditional ink characteristics. By integrating writing pressure information and mathematical context into the modeling process, the team achieved state-of-the-art performance. The proposed method, which utilizes fusion data alongside specific symbol knowledge, significantly outperforms existing benchmarks, which currently lag approximately 20% behind our results. Furthermore, this approach demonstrates robust generalization when applied to drafts, allowing accurate identification even with limited visible ink.

Instead of using probabilistic models, duration averages were calculated across a massive corpus to inform the system. Results indicate that the initial outputs generated using this deterministic approach were of poor quality. However, the integration of duration refinement with Unit Selection Synthesis (USS) significantly enhanced output quality. A critical finding of the study is that even after refinement, the system produces Self-Synthesized Speech (USSS) that acoustically and linguistically diverges from standard Human-Memory-Matched Synthesis (HMM-Synthesis). Consequently, HMM-derived acoustic models were utilized to HMM-Synthesize these self-generated speech samples, facilitating the training of a new, duration-aware Model for HMM-Synsynthetic models (MMTS). Spatial modeling of animal presence/absence data is vital for understanding distribution drivers and setting conservation priorities, yet it remains susceptible to spatial autocorrelation and scale dependency. To address these issues, this work introduces **spHabitat**, an R package that implements spatial models utilizing intrinsic stationary and non-stationary Independent Gaussian Processes (IGPs) based on spatial IGP approaches. Available at `CRAN` and `Bioconductor`, spHabitat offers an accessible entry point for researchers to apply IGP-based IGP modeling to animal spatial data. The package supports univariate, multivariate, and integrated spatial modeling frameworks, available in spatial IGP approaches. Available at `CRAN` and Bioconductor versions of spHabitat offer an easy-to-use interface for implementing IGP approaches in spatial modeling animal presence/absence data. The package provides functions to fit spatial models, predict outcomes, diagnose model fit issues, and compare models using information criteria or spatial predictive ability metrics.
